title: Indra's net
hook: a net of jewels, each reflecting all the others

segments.voice: Yesterday, Autumn Floods: the river met the sea, and the sea called itself a pebble on a mountain. Your line was the sea. Did you find any big water? Today, awe at the other end of the scale: not one vast thing, but countless small ones, each holding all the rest. Day one thousand fourteen.

At night, a window turns into a mirror. Stand in a lit room and look out, and there you are, with the lamp behind you, and the lamp's reflection in the glass of a picture frame, and the frame in the window too. Light bouncing from one surface into the next. Most of the time we don't notice it. Buddhist teachers tell of a net that does this on purpose, and on a scale with no edges. It hangs over the palace of Indra, a king of the gods in old Indian stories. Its name is Indra's net.
screen: `A WINDOW TURNS INTO A MIRROR.` → `LIGHT BOUNCING SURFACE TO SURFACE.` → `A NET OVER INDRA'S PALACE.`

segments.voice: The picture is linked to the Avatamsaka Sutra, a Mahayana Buddhist scripture, and Buddhist teachers have opened it up step by step. First, the net. It stretches out in every direction, with no edge. At each knot where the threads cross hangs a jewel. Clear, polished, shining. Second, the reflection. Look closely into any one jewel, and you'll see in its surface all the other jewels of the net. Not one or two. All of them. Third, the reflection inside the reflection. Each of those reflected jewels is also reflecting all the others. So in the one jewel you're looking at, you see the whole net, and inside every jewel in that picture, the whole net again, and again, without end. One holds all, and all hold the one. Fourth, why the teachers use it. It's a picture of how things are, they say. Nothing exists on its own. Each thing is made of its connections, the way a jewel's whole look comes from what it reflects. Buddhist teaching calls this dependent arising: things come to be because of other things. A modern Zen teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, gave the idea a plainer name, interbeing, and pointed at a sheet of paper. In it, he said, you can see the tree, the rain, the logger, the sun. Some teachers find a comfort in the net. No jewel is lost in a huge web. Each one is a place where the whole web shows up, the one next to it as much as any.
screen: `A JEWEL AT EVERY KNOT.` · `EACH ONE REFLECTS ALL THE OTHERS.` · `THE NET INSIDE EACH REFLECTION.` · `NOTHING EXISTS ON ITS OWN.` · then, large: `EACH REFLECTS ALL.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to notice how one thing reflects many. Find something shiny near you: the back of a spoon, a glass of water, a dark screen, a window. Hold it still, and look into its surface. Count nothing; just notice what's in there. The lamp. A corner of the room. Your own face, bent and small. Then turn it a little, and watch a whole new room slide in. Let the one shiny thing be a jewel in the net, holding everything around it. If you pray, you can give thanks for any of what you see. The bell holds the time.
Indra's net. A Buddhist image: an endless net with a jewel at each knot, each jewel reflecting all the others. Today's word.
Your line: each reflects all. Today, when you catch your reflection in a window or a spoon, notice everything else that shows up in it with you. Day one thousand fourteen.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers, especially in the Huayan and Zen traditions of East Asia, use Indra's net to teach dependent arising: that each thing exists through its connections to everything else.

notes: The fully developed image of the jewel net (each jewel reflecting all others, endlessly) is chiefly from Huayan commentators (Dushun, Fazang) drawing on the Avatamsaka Sutra; the sutra itself mentions Indra's net in places. The teach says 'linked to the Avatamsaka Sutra' and 'Buddhist teachers have opened it up' to stay within what is certain. A Keeper should confirm and may want the Huayan school named in the voice.
'Indra, a king of the gods in old Indian stories': confirm phrasing (Indra is king of the devas in Vedic and Buddhist cosmology).
'Dependent arising' as the doctrine the net illustrates: standard reading; confirm. Huayan's 'one in all, all in one' used in trapdoor.
Thich Nhat Hanh's sheet-of-paper teaching on interbeing paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the details (cloud/rain, tree, logger, sunshine).
howItsDone 'especially in the Huayan and Zen traditions of East Asia' is a judgment; confirm or trim.
